analysis.one_liner: Narrows the Clean Water Act to exclude most wetlands and groundwater, and makes taxpayers pay landowners double for any property value lost to water rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after referral to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, it got no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Clean Water Act to sharply limit which waters the federal government can protect. Only waters that are navigable or permanently connected to navigable streams, rivers, and lakes would count; most wetlands, seasonal streams, drainage channels, and all groundwater would be left to state regulation. It would also ban federal agencies from entering private property to survey waters without the owner's written consent, and require taxpayers to pay landowners twice the value of any property loss caused by a federal water rule — with the rule suspended until every claim is paid. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners and developers whose land contains wetlands, seasonal streams, or drainage channels would face fewer federal permitting requirements and less federal inspection on their property. Landowners whose property value drops because of a federal water rule would receive double the loss from the issuing agency, paid out of that agency's operating budget.

how_it_helps.text: It would narrow the Clean Water Act to cover only navigable-in-fact waters and permanently connected streams, rivers, and lakes, excluding most wetlands, intermittent streams, and drainage channels.
It would give property owners expedited court review of federal jurisdiction determinations and require written federal consent before entering private land to collect water data.
It would require the federal government to pay landowners twice the value of any loss caused by a water regulation, and to withhold that regulation until all claims are paid.

analysis.who_pays: Downstream communities would bear the cost of weaker federal protection over wetlands, groundwater, and seasonal waters that feed the rivers and lakes people depend on for drinking water and recreation. Taxpayers would fund the double-value compensation payments, and the payment requirement would effectively freeze new federal water rules.

drawbacks.text: Removing wetlands without a continuous surface connection and all groundwater from federal jurisdiction would leave many upstream and seasonal waters unprotected, which can worsen downstream pollution that reaches the waterways people use and drink from.

The requirement to pay landowners twice the measured loss, and to freeze any regulation until every claim is paid, would make it fiscally impossible for agencies to issue new water rules — a cost that ultimately falls on taxpayers.
Requiring written consent before federal officials enter private property would make it much harder to investigate pollution discharges and verify compliance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — protecting landowners from federal overreach — is a real concern, but its design is one-sided. By excluding most wetlands, all groundwater, and any water without a continuous surface connection, it would remove federal pollution controls over waters that feed the streams and rivers people drink from, and its double-value compensation mandate would effectively make new water protections unaffordable for agencies. Congress did not act, so neither these protections for developers nor the rollback of safeguards took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing or vote, dying when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 28, 2021 by Sen. Rand Paul with two Republican cosponsors, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — its only action.
The committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate never considered it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill would have narrowed Clean Water Act protections and imposed a costly double-compensation mandate, the public's existing federal water safeguards are better off with it dead. Developers and landowners who wanted federal water rules rolled back gained nothing, but lost nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing clean water safeguards and the public

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to narrow Clean Water Act jurisdiction and require compensation for affected landowners.

for.name: Sens. Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz
Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it, so it never advanced to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Republican senators ever supported the bill, and no Democrats cosponsored it; it never progressed far enough for a vote that would have revealed the partisan split.

industries.industry: Property developers and real estate interests
industries.note: The bill removes federal permitting requirements over most wetlands and intermittent waters and mandates double compensation for any value lost to federal water rules, lowering the cost and risk of developing previously protected land.
Narrowing federal jurisdiction would ease permitting for activities like drainage, farming, and mining on lands containing wetlands and groundwater, shifting oversight to states.

industries.industry: Environmental regulators and water utilities downstream
industries.note: The EPA and Army Corps would lose authority over groundwater, wetlands without surface connections, and any regulation not expressly authorized by Congress, weakening the federal backbone of water protection.
